Cliff Sosin on the limits of intelligence:

"Superintelligence arrived. You probably didn't notice, because it turned out to be kind of incremental.

I think we overrated intelligence, or misread what it is. 

We hold a thin scatter of facts about the world, and intelligence or reasoning is whatever fills the space between them.

Where the space between the facts behaves well, this is close to godlike. Most of what matters doesn't behave like that. 

The universe is mostly the emergent behavior of complex systems. Stir cream into coffee. Watch a storm build out of nothing but atmospheric temperature differences and water vapor. 

You have to run the thing.

The takeoff story assumed the limit was thinking. It isn't. The limit is contact with reality. 

A smarter reasoner fills the gaps between known facts in simple areas faster and better, but it doesn’t produce new facts.

An AI will hand you a genuinely clever design for a jet turbine blade. It might be far more likely to work than anything your engineers came up with. 

It'll still probably fail, because that’s the base rate at the edge of what anyone knows. The only way to find out is to build the blade and try to break it.

That's the real limit on learning, and it doesn't care how smart you are. Coming up with ideas was never the hard part. The hard part is how fast reality answers them.

Most problems can't be worked out at a desk by thinking. Those stay bound by how fast we can build the thing and see if it holds, and that clock barely moves."

From his essay "Maybe Intelligence Ain't All That." He walks through it here.

Cliff Sosin on why you want to own the complements to cheap intelligence, like Meta does:

"I've found it helpful to assume everyone has really great intelligence and ask what's left. 

If intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, what you want to own are the complements to intelligence. 

The complements are data, attention, love, physical proximity, scale, regulatory capture.

Let's talk about Meta. They have $250 billion of revenue, and they spend $250 billion a year. The question you might ask is, what do they spend it on? A really reductionist view is that they spend it all on intelligence.

They're buying data centers. They're literally buying inference. They're paying really smart people to write algorithms. They're writing code. That's just intelligence.

If you think forward with the fact that the price of intelligence is falling by a factor of a hundred or something over the next five years, their costs kind of go away.

Maybe instead of taking their cost to zero with much better intelligence at much lower prices, maybe they can sell a few more ads.

All of this is downstream of what they possess, which is not destroyed by ubiquitous intelligence, which is data and attention. 

I don't think that the availability of cheap and ubiquitous intelligence is gonna cause people not to be interested in watching funny 20-second videos."

$USDD was the fastest-growing stablecoin in the past week.

At first look, it may seem like a spike from a campaign or yield boost, but there's actually more to it.

@USDDecentralize has spent years building an ecosystem around two things: earning yield & making stablecoin transfers cheaper.

USDD is now earning ~4% APY natively for its holders.

USDD's Smart Allocator puts reserves to work across blue-chip protocols like @aave, @sparkfinance, and @Morpho, earning interest from borrowers and additional protocol rewards.

That revenue is redirected to support the yield.

Meanwhile, GasFree allows USDD transfers on TRON without holding TRX, at 0.5 USDD per transaction versus 1.5 USDT for USDT through GasFree.

Add here Binance, Gate, and JustLend distribution, and you get a self-sustaining growth engine with each piece supporting the other.

Yield gives users a reason to hold USDD, while cheaper transfers make it useful beyond simply sitting in a wallet.

That's a more interesting growth model than attracting deposits with high APYs alone.

Since its expansion from TRON to Ethereum, Ethereum now accounts for 26% of USDD's supply, which gives it another substantial market to attract stablecoin holders beyond TRON's ecosystem.

Definitely a top contender for the top stablecoin spot as a decentralized alternative to Tether and Circle.

Summing up the challenge of commercializing robots in one photo

The bar for both reliability and output quality is much higher for physical labor than it is for knowledge work. A chatbot that produces work that is just “good enough” or low quality can still be useful. 

A mediocre rough draft could still save time because a person can keep what’s good and fix the rest before its final. Copywriting, slides, and contracts can all be edited.

What is considered “good enough” for physical work has much higher standards. A bad weld can ruin metal. A wrong dose given to a patient is unacceptable.

Outputs from work done by humans or robots in the physical often serve as direct inputs into the workflow that are hard to recover from if an error arises. Outputs from work done by humans or Chatbots for knowledge work are much more tolerant of errors and poor quality because supervision can be baked in before the output is used further down the workflow.

The reliability threshold is 2-4 orders of magnitude greater for physical work than knowledge work and it’s what we’ve started to achieve this year. The upside is that by optimizing for reliability, robots will be able to work at a high level of utilization and operate at higher levels of autonomy compared to general purpose AI models in 2023. Machines that can deliver up to 24 hours of work a day as opposed to minutes or hours of work.
